p.src: Baoyu returned to his room and washed his hands, then discussed the matter with Xiren. “When we drink tonight, everyone should enjoy themselves without standing on ceremony. Tell them now what we are to eat, so they can begin preparing it early.” Xiren laughed. “Don't worry. Qingwen, Sheyue, Qiuwen, and I have each put in five qian of silver, making two taels altogether. Fangguan, Bihen, Xiaoyan, and Si'er have each put in three qian—counterfeit coins not included—bringing the total to three taels and two qian. We gave it to Mrs. Liu long ago and ordered forty dishes of fruit and delicacies. I spoke to Ping'er too, and a jar of fine Shaoxing wine has already been carried over and hidden there. The eight of us are giving you a birthday celebration all by ourselves.” Delighted, Baoyu hurriedly said, “Where would they get the money? We ought not to have made them contribute.” Qingwen said, “They have no money, but do you suppose we do? It is each person's own token of affection. Even if they stole it, just accept their kindness and have done with it.” Baoyu laughed. “You are right.” Xiren laughed. “A day never feels complete to you unless she has slapped you down with a couple of sharp words.” Qingwen laughed. “You have learned wicked ways too—always fanning the flames and setting people against each other.” At this, they all laughed. Baoyu said, “Go and shut the courtyard gate.” Xiren laughed. “No wonder people call you a ‘busybody with nothing to do.’ If we shut the gate now, people will grow suspicious. We may as well wait a little longer.” Baoyu nodded and said, “I shall take a walk outside. Si'er, go draw some water; Xiaoyan alone may come with me.” With that, he went outside. Seeing no one about, he asked her about Wu'er. Xiaoyan said, “I told Mrs. Liu just now, and she was delighted. But after the wrong and distress Wu'er suffered that night, she went home and fell ill from anger. How could she come now? We shall simply have to wait until she recovers.” Hearing this, Baoyu could not help regretting it and sighing deeply. Then he asked, “Does Xiren know about this or not?” Xiaoyan said, “I did not tell her. I don't know whether Fangguan has.” Baoyu said, “I have not told her either. Never mind; I shall tell her myself.” Having said this, he went back inside and deliberately washed his hands again.

p.src: It was already time to light the lamps when they heard a group of people entering by the courtyard gate. Everyone peeped silently through the window and saw, as expected, Mrs. Lin Zhixiao approaching with several supervising women, led by someone carrying a large lantern. Qingwen whispered with a smile, “They have come to inspect the night watch. Once they leave, we can shut the gate.” All those on night duty at Happy Red Court went out to meet them, and Mrs. Lin Zhixiao inspected every one. Mrs. Lin Zhixiao warned them, “Do not gamble or drink, then tumble into bed and sleep until broad daylight. If I hear of it, I shall not tolerate it.” They all laughed. “Who would ever dare to do such a thing?” Mrs. Lin Zhixiao then asked, “Has Second Master Bao gone to bed?” They all replied that they did not know. Xiren hastily nudged Baoyu. Baoyu slipped into his shoes and came out to greet her. “I have not gone to bed yet. Come inside and rest a while, mother.” Then he called, “Xiren, bring some tea.” Mrs. Lin Zhixiao hurried inside and said with a smile, “Still awake? The days are long and the nights short now. You ought to retire early so that you can rise early tomorrow. Otherwise, if you rise late tomorrow, people will laugh and say that instead of being a young gentleman devoted to his studies, you are no better than a common porter.” Having said this, she laughed again. Baoyu hurriedly smiled. “You are quite right, mother. I go to bed early every day. Whenever you come in, I am already asleep and know nothing of it. Today I ate noodles and was afraid they might sit heavily on my stomach, so I stayed up to amuse myself a little longer.” Mrs. Lin Zhixiao then said smilingly to Xiren and the others, “You should brew him some Pu'er tea.” Xiren and Qingwen hastily replied with smiles, “We brewed a pot of Nü'er tea, and he has already drunk two bowls. Have a bowl yourself, auntie; it is all ready.” As she spoke, Qingwen poured out a bowl and brought it over. Mrs. Lin Zhixiao smiled again. “Lately I have heard Second Master changing the way he addresses these senior maids and calling them directly by name. Though they serve in this room, they are ultimately the Old Lady's and the Lady's people, so you should still address them with due respect. It does no harm to call a name once in a while, but if you do it constantly, your younger brothers and nephews may imitate you. Then people will laugh and say that no one in this family respects their elders.” Baoyu smiled. “You are right, mother. I have only ever done it now and then.” Xiren and Qingwen both laughed. “You must not accuse him unjustly in this. Even now, he never stops calling us ‘sister.’ Only while we are playing does he call us by name once or twice; in front of others, he addresses us just as he always did.” Mrs. Lin Zhixiao smiled. “That is as it should be. That is the conduct of one who studies and understands propriety.”

p.src: The humbler and more respectful he is himself, the more he deserves the name of a gentleman. He would never lightly mistreat an old servant of three or five generations' standing, or one newly transferred from the Old Lady's or Madam's apartments—not even a cat or dog belonging to their rooms. That is how a properly brought-up young gentleman conducts himself.” When she had finished, she drank her tea and said, “Please retire now. We shall be going.” Baoyu still urged her, “Stay a little longer.” But Lin Zhixiao's wife had already led the others away to inspect the other quarters. Qingwen and the others hurriedly had the gate shut, then came in laughing. “That good lady must have had a cup somewhere. She prattled on and on and gave us a fine scolding before she left.” Sheyue laughed. “She meant well. After all, she has to remind us of these things from time to time. She only wants to guard against some serious mishap.” As she spoke, the wine and fruit were set out. Xiren said, “There is no need to sit around a formal table. Let us put that round rosewood kang-table on the kang and sit there. It will be roomier and more convenient.” At her suggestion, they duly carried it over. Sheyue and Si'er went to fetch the fruit, making four or five trips with two large tea trays before they had brought it all in. Two old serving-women squatted outside beside a brazier, warming and straining the wine. Baoyu said, “It is hot. We should all take off our outer clothes.” The others laughed. “Take yours off if you wish. We still have to take turns formally seating the guests.” Baoyu laughed. “If you begin all that seating ceremony, it will last until the fifth watch. You know how I detest such conventions. Before outsiders they cannot be helped, but you should not plague me with them now.” Hearing this, they all said, “We shall do as you wish.” So instead of taking their seats at once, they busied themselves removing their ornaments and loosening their clothes.

p.src: Presently they had removed their formal attire. Their hair was merely twisted into casual knots, and they all wore long skirts with short jackets. Baoyu wore only a little bright-red jacket of wadded gauze and green satin lined trousers patterned with splashed ink, their legs left loose. Reclining against a new pale-jade gauze-covered pillow stuffed with rose and peony petals of every hue, he began playing the finger-guessing game with Fangguan. Fangguan kept complaining of the heat. She wore only a little patchwork lined jacket made of pale-jade, dark-red, and tawny velvet and satin, with a willow-green sash at her waist and pale-red flower-sprigged lined trousers below, their legs also left loose. A ring of tiny braids ran around her brow and temples, all gathered at the crown into a single braid as thick as a goose egg, which hung down behind her head. In her right earlobe was only a tiny jade plug the size of a grain of rice, while from her left hung a single large hard-red pendant, gold-mounted and as big as a ginkgo nut. These made her face seem whiter than the full moon and her eyes clearer than autumn water. The sight made everyone laugh. “Those two really look like twin brothers!” Xiren and the others poured wine for each in turn. “Wait a little before playing the finger game. Though we are not holding a formal banquet, each of you must at least take a sip from our hands.” Xiren went first, raising the cup to her lips and taking a sip; the rest followed in order, each drinking in turn, and only then did they all settle into a circle. There was no room for Xiaoyan and Si'er on the edge of the kang. So they brought over two chairs and placed them close beside it. The forty little dishes were all alike, made of white Ding ware, and no bigger than small tea saucers. Yet they held every kind of delicacy, fruit, and vegetable under heaven—from north and south of the mountains, from the Central Plain and foreign lands, dried or fresh, from water or land. Baoyu said, “We ought to play a drinking game too.” Xiren said, “It had better be something refined. Do not shout and make such a din that others hear us. Besides, we cannot read, so do not choose anything too literary.” Sheyue laughed. “Let us throw dice and compete for reds.” Baoyu said, “That is dull. No. Let us draw flower names.” Qingwen laughed. “Exactly! I have long wanted to try that game.” Xiren said, “It is a fine game, but it will be no fun with so few people.” Xiaoyan laughed. “In my opinion, we should quietly invite Miss Bao and Miss Lin to join us for a while. It will not be too late to sleep when the second watch comes.” Xiren said, “You will make another commotion opening doors and calling from house to house. What if the night watch meets you and asks what you are doing?” Baoyu said, “What is there to fear? Third Sister drinks too; we should invite her as well. And Miss Qin as well.” They all said, “Better leave Miss Qin out of it. She is in the Young Mistress's apartments; calling her out would cause far too much commotion.” Baoyu said, “What is there to fear? Hurry and invite them.”

Xiren and the others poured several more large beakers and heaped plates with assorted fruits and dishes for the old matrons sitting below. Fangguan’s cheeks were as red as rouge, and intoxication lent still more charm to her brows and eyes. Unable to support herself, she collapsed against Xiren. “Dear sister, my heart is pounding so!” Xiren laughed. “Who told you to pour it down with all your might?” Xiaoyan and Si’er, likewise unable to hold themselves up, had already fallen asleep. Seeing that Fangguan was very drunk, Xiren feared she might be sick and vomit over her. She therefore rose gently, helped Fangguan to Baoyu’s side, and left her there to sleep. p.src: They all sank into a deep, sweet sleep, oblivious to everything. When day broke, Xiren opened her eyes and saw the sky shining brightly. “How late it is!” she exclaimed. Glancing toward the bed opposite, she saw Fangguan still asleep with her head resting against the edge of the kang, and hurriedly rose to wake her. Baoyu had already turned over and awakened. Laughing, he said, “It really is late!” He then gave Fangguan another push to rouse her. Fangguan sat up, still dazed and rubbing her eyes. Xiren laughed. “Have you no shame? We may fairly claim to know how to drink, seeing how we emptied that whole jar of wine. Just when the fun was at its height, there was none left.” Xiren laughed. “That is precisely what made it enjoyable. If we had carried on until all our high spirits were spent, it would have left no lingering pleasure. Yesterday everyone became thoroughly merry; even Qingwen forgot her modesty, and I remember that she sang a song.” Si'er laughed. “You have forgotten, sister—you sang one too. Who at the banquet did not sing?” At this they all blushed, clasping their hands together as they laughed without end.

p.src: Having reached this conclusion, Baoyu slipped the card into his sleeve and went straight to find Daiyu. He had just passed Dripping Fragrance Pavilion when he suddenly saw Xiuyan approaching with tottering steps. Baoyu hurriedly asked, “Where are you going, cousin?” Xiuyan smiled. “I am going to talk with Miaoyu.” Baoyu was astonished to hear this. “She is solitary and eccentric, quite out of step with the world, and scarcely one person in ten thousand meets with her approval. So she thinks highly of you! She plainly knows that you are no ordinary person like the rest of us.” Xiuyan smiled. “It is not necessarily because she truly esteems me. We were neighbors for ten years, with only a wall between us. She practiced religious cultivation at Incense Coil Temple. My family was poor and rented rooms belonging to the temple; we lived there for ten years, and whenever I had nothing to do, I went over to keep her company. Everything I know of reading and writing, I learned from her. We were friends from days of poverty and low estate, and she was also half a teacher to me. After my family left to seek refuge with relatives, I heard that her unconventional ways had made her intolerable to the powerful, so she eventually came here for shelter. Now, by another providential coincidence, we have met again, and our former affection has not changed. Indeed, she looks on me even more favorably than before.” To Baoyu, this revelation came like a thunderclap. Delighted, he laughed and said, “No wonder your every gesture and word is as untrammeled as a wild crane among drifting clouds! Now I see where it comes from. Something concerning her has put me in a quandary, and I was just going to ask someone’s advice. Meeting you now is truly a heaven-sent coincidence. Please tell me what to do.” With that, he took out the visiting card and showed it to Xiuyan. Xiuyan smiled. “She really cannot change that temperament of hers. She was born this wildly unconventional and perversely eccentric. I have never before seen anyone put an assumed style on a visiting card. As the saying goes, she is ‘neither nun nor laywoman, neither woman nor man.’ What sense does that make?” Baoyu hastily replied with a smile, “You do not understand. She cannot be counted among ordinary people at all; she stands beyond all worldly expectations. She sent me this card only because she takes me for someone with at least a little understanding. I could not decide what wording to use in my reply and was just going to ask Cousin Lin when, by good fortune, I met you.” On hearing this, Xiuyan carefully looked Baoyu up and down for quite some time before smiling. “No wonder they say that meeting a person is better than merely hearing of him. No wonder Miaoyu sent you this card, and no wonder she gave you those plum blossoms last year. Since even she treats you so, I had better explain the reason to you. She often says, ‘From the Han and Jin through the Five Dynasties, Tang, and Song, none of the ancients wrote good poetry. There are only two good lines: “Though an iron threshold last a thousand years, in the end one earthen mound awaits.”’ That is why she calls herself ‘the Person Outside the Threshold.’ She also constantly praises Zhuangzi’s writings above all others, and so at times calls herself ‘the Eccentric.’

p.src: Later, seeing that Fangguan had dressed her hair in a knot and adorned it with flowers and kingfisher-feather ornaments, Baoyu promptly ordered her to change her appearance. He had the short hair around her head shaved off to reveal the blue-green scalp and the hair parted broadly down the middle. He added, “In winter, wear a large sable ‘sleeping hare’ cap; on your feet, wear little multicolored battle boots with tiger-head and coiling-cloud designs. Or leave your trouser legs loose and wear only clean socks and thick-soled, bound shoes.” Then he said, “The name Fangguan is no good. It would be more distinctive if we changed it to a man’s name.” So he renamed her Xiongnu, ‘Bold Slave.’ Fangguan was thoroughly delighted. “If that is how it is, take me with you whenever you go out. If anyone asks, just say I am a page like Mingyan.” Baoyu laughed. “People would still see through you.” Fangguan laughed. “That is why I say you have no ingenuity. Several families of native border people live on our estate. Just say that I am a little native girl. Besides, everyone says I look good with my hair in linked braids. What do you think of that idea?” Baoyu was unexpectedly delighted by this suggestion and hastily laughed. “That is an excellent idea! I have often seen officials attended by members of foreign peoples once presented as captives, because they can withstand wind and frost and are nimble on horseback. In that case, let us give you a foreign name as well: Yelü Xiongnu. The two syllables ‘Xiongnu’—‘Bold Slave’— also echo the name of the Xiongnu; both are names belonging to the western tribes. Moreover, these two peoples have been a scourge to China since the age of Yao and Shun, and the Jin, Tang, and other dynasties suffered grievously at their hands. Fortunately, we are blessed to have been born in the present age. Our sovereign is the true descendant of great Shun; his sage virtue, benevolence, and filial piety blaze so splendidly that they move Heaven and shall endure for countless ages with Heaven, Earth, sun, and moon. Thus all the leaping, rampaging clowns of former dynasties have now, without the use of a single shield or spear, been made by Heaven to fold their hands, bow their heads, and come from afar to submit. We ought indeed to make sport of them, thereby adding luster to our sovereign and father.” Fangguan laughed. “If that is so, you ought to practice archery and horsemanship, learn some martial skills, stride boldly forth, and capture a few rebels. Would that not be serving your sovereign with loyalty? Why must you make use of us, wagging your tongue and amusing yourself with playacting, yet claiming that you are celebrating glorious achievements and praising imperial virtue?” Baoyu laughed. “That only shows that you do not understand. Now the whole realm has submitted and every quarter is at peace; for a thousand years, even ten thousand, there will be no need for arms. Even in our games and laughter, we ought to sing the praises of the age, lest we prove unworthy of peacefully enjoying its prosperity.” Fangguan found his reasoning sound, and the two of them considered the arrangement perfectly apt. From then on, Baoyu called her “Yelü Xiongnu.”

p.src: In fact, both branches of the Jia family had among their servants prisoners whom their ancestors had captured and been granted as slaves; but they were fit only to tend horses and could not be entrusted with important duties. Xiangyun had always been exceptionally fond of boisterous play, and especially liked dressing as a warrior; she would often fasten a jeweled belt around herself and put on a costume with narrow sleeves. Recently, seeing Baoyu dress Fangguan as a boy, she had dressed Kuiguan as a lad as well. Kuiguan already kept her hair closely cropped so that stage makeup and greasepaint could easily be applied to her face, and she was nimble of hand and foot; thus one step in dressing her was already saved. Li Wan and Tanchun were delighted when they saw her, and had Baoqin's Douguan dressed as a little page too, with two girlish topknots, a short jacket, and red shoes. Except for the painted face, she looked exactly like a young zither attendant on the stage. Xiangyun renamed Kuiguan, calling her “Daying.” Since her surname was Wei, Xiangyun called her Wei Daying, which suited her fancy, for it secretly alluded to the saying, “Only a great hero can show his true colors.” Why should a man need rouge and powder? Douguan was extremely small in both stature and age, and exceedingly quick-witted and mischievous; hence her name, Douguan, or “Bean.” Some in the Garden called her “Little Dou,” while others called her “Fried Bean.” Baoqin, however, said that names like Zither Boy and Book Boy were too commonplace, whereas the word dou was distinctive; so she renamed her “Dou童,” or “Bean Boy.” After the meal, when Ping'er returned the banquet, she remarked that Red Fragrance Enclosure was too hot, so several tables of fresh wine and fine dishes were set out in Elm Shade Hall. To everyone's delight, Madam You came over to enjoy herself too, bringing Peifeng and Xieyuan, her husband's two concubines. These two concubines too were young, pretty, and artlessly playful, though they seldom came there. Now that they had entered the Garden and met Xiangyun, Xiangling, Fangrui, and the other girls, the sayings “people of a kind gather together” and “things divide according to their kind” proved perfectly true. They talked and laughed without end, paying no heed to where Madam You was; leaving the maids to attend her, they went about amusing themselves with each of the others. When they presently reached Happy Red Court, they suddenly heard Baoyu call out “Yelü Xiongnu.” Peifeng, Xieyuan, and Xiangling collapsed together in laughter and asked what the words meant. Everyone began imitating the name, but they either mispronounced it or forgot some of its syllables, until some even called out “wild donkey,” making everyone in the Garden who heard it double up with laughter. Seeing everyone mock her, Baoyu feared they would humiliate her and hurriedly said, “I have heard that in the far western land of France there is a precious aventurine glass, which in the language of that country is called ‘Wendurina.’ Now I shall compare you to that jewel and rename you ‘Wendurina.’ How would you like that?” Fangguan was even more delighted when she heard this and said, “Yes, let it be so.” And so they began calling her by this name as well. But the others found it awkward to pronounce, so they translated it back into Chinese and simply called her “Boli,” or “Glass.”

p.src: While the merriment was still at its height, several people from the eastern mansion suddenly came running up in alarm and cried, “The master has passed away!” Everyone was badly startled and exclaimed, “He was perfectly well and had no illness. How could he suddenly be dead?” The servants replied, “The master practiced cultivation every day. He must have perfected his merit and ascended as an immortal.” On hearing this, Madam You realized that Jia Zhen and his son, as well as Jia Lian and the other men, were all away from home, leaving not a single reliable man at hand, and she was naturally thrown into confusion. She had no choice but to remove her ornaments at once and send men ahead to Xuanzhen Temple to lock up all the Taoist priests until the young master returned to question them. Meanwhile, she hurriedly took a carriage out of the city with Lai Sheng and a group of male and female household servants. She also summoned imperial physicians to determine what illness had caused his death. The physicians could hardly take the pulse of a dead man. They had long known that Jia Jing's breathing exercises were wholly absurd, and that his worship of the stars, keeping vigil on the night of Gengshen, and swallowing cinnabar elixirs were all deluded and futile practices. The excessive mental and physical strain had instead cost him his life. Even in death, his abdomen was hard as iron, while the skin of his face and his lips had been burned dark purple and were wrinkled and cracked. They therefore reported to Madam You, “He died from burning and swelling caused by swallowing gold and taking cinnabar in accordance with Taoist teachings.” The Taoist priests protested in alarm, “The trouble was caused by an elixir of cinnabar that the master had recently prepared by a secret method. We humble Taoists did warn him, ‘You must not take it before your spiritual merit is complete.’ But unexpectedly, while keeping vigil on Gengshen tonight, the master swallowed it in secret and ascended as an immortal. Surely, through sincere devotion, he attained the Way, escaped the sea of suffering, cast off his mortal shell, and departed to liberation.” Madam You refused to listen. She merely ordered that they remain locked up until Jia Zhen returned to dispose of the matter, and sent a rider galloping to deliver the news. Seeing that the place was too cramped to keep the body, and that in any case it could not be taken into the city, she hastily had it shrouded and carried in a sedan chair to Iron Threshold Temple, where it was laid out. By her reckoning, it would be at least half a month before Jia Zhen could arrive. As the weather was now intensely hot and the body could not possibly be kept until then, she took charge herself and ordered an astrologer to choose a date for encoffinment. Fortunately, his coffin had been prepared years before and stored at this temple, which made matters much easier. Three days later, formal mourning began and the household donned mourning dress. Meanwhile, Taoist funeral rites were begun as they waited for Jia Zhen.

p.src: Now when Jia Zhen heard the news, he immediately requested leave; Jia Rong, too, held an official post. The Ministry of Rites, knowing how greatly the present Emperor esteemed filial and fraternal devotion, dared not decide the matter on its own and submitted a memorial requesting an imperial ruling. The Emperor was in fact exceptionally benevolent and filial and showed particular regard for the descendants of meritorious ministers. Upon seeing the memorial, he at once asked what office Jia Jing had held. The Ministry of Rites replied on his behalf: “He obtained the presented-scholar degree, while the hereditary office of his forebears has already passed by privilege to his son Jia Zhen. Because Jia Jing was advanced in years and frequently ill, he generally lived in quiet retirement at the Xuanzhen Temple outside the capital. He has now died there of illness. His son Zhen and grandson Rong are presently here in attendance upon Your Majesty during the national mourning and therefore request leave to return and encoffin him.” On hearing this, the Emperor promptly issued a special decree of grace: “Although Jia Jing was a commoner and rendered no service to the state, in consideration of the merits of his forefathers he is posthumously granted an office of the fifth rank. His descendants shall escort his coffin into the capital through the northern lower gate and conduct the funeral rites at his private residence. After his descendants have performed all the mourning rites, they may escort the coffin back to their ancestral home; moreover, the Court of Imperial Entertainments shall provide sacrifices according to precedent. All at court, from princes and dukes downward, are permitted to offer sacrifices and condolences. Respect this.” Once this decree was issued, not only did the Jia household express its gratitude for the imperial favor, but all the ministers at court repeatedly acclaimed and praised the Emperor. Jia Zhen and his son galloped back through the night. Halfway home they encountered Jia Pin and Jia Guang riding swiftly toward them with a band of household servants. At the sight of Jia Zhen, both men tumbled from their saddles and came forward to pay their respects. Jia Zhen hastily asked, “What are you doing here?” Jia Pin replied, “Sister-in-law feared that once you and your nephew had returned, the old lady would have no one to attend her on the journey, so she sent the two of us to escort her.” Jia Zhen praised this arrangement without end, then asked how matters were being managed at home. Jia Pin and the others told him how the Taoists had been detained and the body moved to the family temple, and how, for fear that no one would be at home to receive them, his mother-in-law and the two younger aunts had been brought to stay in the principal rooms. Jia Rong now dismounted as well, and on hearing that the two young aunts had arrived, exchanged a smile with Jia Zhen. Jia Zhen hurriedly said several times, “Excellent, excellent,” then applied the whip and rode on. Without stopping at an inn, they changed horses through the night and galloped onward. One day they reached the capital gate and made first for Iron Threshold Temple. It was already the fourth watch. When the night watchman learned of their arrival, he hastily roused everyone. Jia Zhen dismounted and, together with Jia Rong, burst into loud wailing. From outside the main gate they crawled forward on their knees, and on reaching the coffin they knocked their foreheads to the ground and wept as though shedding blood. They did not stop until daybreak, when their voices had grown hoarse. Lady You and the others all came to meet them. Jia Zhen and his son promptly changed into mourning clothes according to ritual and prostrated themselves before the coffin. Yet, since they themselves had to manage affairs, they could not entirely shut their eyes and ears to everything around them. They were obliged to moderate their grief somewhat so that they could direct the others. He then recounted the imperial decree in full to all the relatives and friends. Meanwhile, he first sent Jia Rong home to arrange for the coffin to lie in state. Jia Rong was only too glad to receive the order. He galloped home ahead of the others and promptly commanded that the tables and chairs be removed from the front hall, the lattice partitions taken down, mourning draperies hung, and a musicians’ pavilion and ceremonial arch erected before the gate, among other preparations.

Jia Pin and the others told him how the Taoists had been detained and the body moved to the family temple, and how, for fear that no one would be at home to receive them, his mother-in-law and the two younger aunts had been brought to stay in the principal rooms.
Jia Rong now dismounted as well, and on hearing that the two young aunts had arrived, exchanged a smile with Jia Zhen.
Jia Zhen hurriedly said several times, “Excellent, excellent,” then applied the whip and rode on. Without stopping at an inn, they changed horses through the night and galloped onward.
One day they reached the capital gate and made first for Iron Threshold Temple.
It was already the fourth watch. When the night watchman learned of their arrival, he hastily roused everyone.

Jia Zhen dismounted and, together with Jia Rong, burst into loud wailing. From outside the main gate they crawled forward on their knees, and on reaching the coffin they knocked their foreheads to the ground and wept as though shedding blood. They did not stop until daybreak, when their voices had grown hoarse.
Lady You and the others all came to meet them.

Jia Zhen and his son promptly changed into mourning clothes according to ritual and prostrated themselves before the coffin. Yet, since they themselves had to manage affairs, they could not entirely shut their eyes and ears to everything around them. They were obliged to moderate their grief somewhat so that they could direct the others.
He then recounted the imperial decree in full to all the relatives and friends.
Meanwhile, he first sent Jia Rong home to arrange for the coffin to lie in state.

Jia Rong was only too glad to receive the order. He galloped home ahead of the others and promptly commanded that the tables and chairs be removed from the front hall, the lattice partitions taken down, mourning draperies hung, and a musicians’ pavilion and ceremonial arch erected before the gate, among other preparations.

p.src: He then hurried inside to see his maternal grandmother and his two young aunts. Old Lady You was advanced in years and fond of sleep, and usually reclined at ease. His second and third aunts were doing needlework with the maids. When he entered, they all complained that he had come to make a nuisance of himself. Jia Rong grinned at his second aunt and said, “Second Aunt, here you are again! Our father has been longing for you.” Second Sister You blushed and scolded him: “You young wretch Rong! If I go two days without giving you a scolding, you simply cannot behave yourself. You grow more shameless and ill-mannered by the day. And to think you are the young master of a great family, studying books and rites every day! Your manners are now worse even than those of some ill-bred brat from a petty household.” As she spoke, she picked up an iron and swung it straight at his head. Jia Rong was so frightened that he covered his head and tumbled into her arms, begging for mercy. Third Sister You came forward to pinch his mouth and added, “When our elder sister comes home, we shall tell her about you.”

p.src: Jia Rong hastily knelt laughing on the kang and begged forgiveness, at which the two sisters laughed again. Jia Rong then fought with his second aunt over some cardamom seeds. Second Sister You chewed up a mouthful of husks and spat them all over his face. Jia Rong licked it all up with his tongue and ate it. The maids could bear the sight no longer and said with a laugh, “You are still in the first heat of mourning, and the old lady has only just fallen asleep. Young though they may be, they are still your aunts by marriage. You show far too little respect for your wife. When she returns, we shall tell the master, and then you will have more than you can handle.” Jia Rong left his aunts alone, embraced the maids, and kissed them. “My darlings, you are right. Let us speak ill of those two.” The maids hurriedly pushed him away and angrily scolded him: “You short-lived devil! You have a wife and maids of your own, yet you insist on fooling with us. Those who know you will say you are only playing, but if some foul-hearted, rotten-gutted busybody and gossip sees us and spreads the story, who in that other mansion will not hear of it? Who will not whisper behind our backs that everything here is in disorder?” Jia Rong laughed. “Each household has its own gate; who has any business meddling in another’s affairs? Everyone has enough affairs of his own to occupy him. From ancient times to the present, people have even spoken of the ‘filthy Tang and stinking Han’ dynasties. How much more so with a family such as ours! What family has no amorous scandals? Do not make me tell you about them. Strict as the Elder Master is over there, even Uncle Lian has had an improper affair with that young concubine. And strong-willed as Miss Feng is, Uncle Rui still had designs on her. Not one of these things has been kept from me!”

p.src: As Jia Rong went on talking wild nonsense at random, he saw that his grandmother had awakened, so he paid his respects, asked after her health, and said, “It has been a great trouble to the Old Ancestress, and our two aunts have also had to suffer much hardship. My father and I can never be grateful enough. Once everything is over, every member of our household, old and young, will come to your door and kowtow in thanks.” Old Madam You nodded. “My dear boy, you certainly know how to speak properly. It is only right for relatives to help one another.” Then she asked, “Is your father well? When did he receive the news and hurry back?” Jia Rong laughed. “He arrived just now and sent me first to see how you were. He begs you, whatever you do, not to leave until everything is over.” As he spoke, he winked at his second aunt. Second Sister You quietly gritted her teeth and, smiling, scolded him: “You glib-tongued little monkey! Do you mean to keep us here to become mothers to your father?” Jia Rong teased his grandmother again. “Don’t worry. Every day my father frets over my two aunts and tries to find two prospective uncles for them—men of good family, rich and noble, young and handsome—so that he can marry both aunts off properly. For the past few years he has never managed to choose anyone, but as luck would have it, only the other day he spotted a suitable man on the road.” Old Madam You took him seriously and hurriedly asked whose family the man belonged to. The two sisters dropped what they were doing and, laughing all the while, chased Jia Rong and tried to hit him. They cried, “Mother, don’t believe this wretch who deserves to be struck by lightning!” Even the maids said, “Heaven has eyes—mind you aren’t struck by lightning!” Just then someone came to report, “The business is finished. Would the young master please go out and inspect it, then report back to the master?” Only then did Jia Rong go off, still grinning. What happened next remains unknown; listen to the next chapter for the explanation.
